Licensing & Monetization

Licensing & Monetization allows third-party engineers to create paid Behaviors and Controllers that integrate directly into the pipeline. Vendors retain full control over license validation, while Vault enforces deterministic execution rules at runtime.

This page is a practical guide for engineers building monetized extensions. It explains the required contracts, shows complete examples, and outlines the runtime guarantees your extension can rely on.

Note

Vault does not validate licenses. Vault enforces pipeline decisions based on validation results you provide. You own cryptographic verification, remote calls, retries, and token parsing. Vault owns enforcement.

Note

Licensing is not active when devMode is set to true.  See more →

Why Build a Monetized Extension?

is designed to be extensible. Engineers frequently build specialized Behaviors and Controllers that provide unique value—advanced persistence strategies, encryption layers, analytics pipelines, compliance tooling, policy engines, or domain-specific orchestration logic.

If that extension represents proprietary expertise or commercial value, you may choose to distribute it under a paid license. The Vault licensing mechanism exists to support that model in a deterministic, enforcement-safe way.

The Business Flow Is Yours

Vault does not manage commerce, billing, subscriptions, customer records, or entitlements. Those responsibilities belong entirely to you as the vendor.

A typical monetization flow looks like this:

You are responsible for:

  • Defining your commercial license agreement
  • Issuing license keys or signed payloads
  • Handling payments, renewals, and entitlement tracking
  • Implementing cryptographic or remote validation logic
  • Retry logic and network resilience
  • Providing customer support for licensing and activation issues
  • Maintaining and updating your extension over time
  • Monitoring security advisories and keeping dependencies (e.g., npm packages) up to date

Vault’s role is limited and intentional:

  • Track license state
  • Prevent spoofed validation
  • Enforce deterministic pipeline activation or denial
  • Guarantee timeout safety

In short: You control entitlement. Vault controls enforcement.

What You Are Building
↑ top

A monetized extension in is a licensed Behavior or Controller that participates in the pipeline only after successful validation.

Technically, your extension must:

  • Declare needsLicense: true in its decorator
  • Provide a licenseId that matches the customer’s Vault configuration
  • Extend LicensingAbstract
  • Call validateLicense(true | false)

Activation Rules

  • If validation succeeds → the FeatureCell activates normally.
  • If validation fails → the FeatureCell is terminal.
  • If validation never occurs → timeout → terminal.

If a FeatureCell contains multiple licensed extensions, all must validate successfully. A single failure makes the entire FeatureCell terminal.

If a FeatureCell contains no licensed extensions, it activates automatically.

Deterministic Enforcement

Once denied, the FeatureCell cannot be reactivated without full reinitialization. Vault behaves as a one-way state machine to guarantee deterministic outcomes.

How to Build a Monetized Extension
↑ top

Building a licensed Behavior or Controller is more than adding needsLicense: true. It requires defining your validation strategy, selling and issuing licenses to customers, and integrating your extension with Vault’s enforcement model.

The sections below outline the complete vendor lifecycle — from selling a license to activating a FeatureCell at runtime.

  • Design Your Validation Strategy
    Decide how licenses will be verified (public/private key cryptography, signed tokens, remote API validation, etc.).
  • Sell and Issue the License
    Define your commercial flow: customer purchase, key generation, entitlement tracking, and expiration or revocation rules.
  • Define the License Payload
    Determine what data the customer must provide to Vault (token, signature, headers, metadata, etc.).
  • Instruct the Customer How to Configure Vault
    Document how they supply your licenseId and payload via provideVault().
  • Required Contract
    Declare needsLicense: true, define your licenseId, and extend LicensingAbstract.
  • Licensing Runtime Integration
    Understand how Vault injects license payloads and how your extension reports validation results.
  • Example: Licensed Behavior
    Implement validation inside a Behavior.
  • Example: Licensed Controller
    Apply the same licensing mechanism to Controllers.
  • Asynchronous Validation
    Perform remote or cryptographic verification safely within the timeout window.
  • Runtime Guarantees
    Understand queueing, denial rules, and terminal enforcement.
  • License Enforcement Outcomes
    Understand how validation results activate or deny a FeatureCell.
  • Architectural Guarantees
    Review the strict responsibility boundaries between Vault and Vendor.
  • Failure Handling & Observability
    Learn how denial surfaces to the global error handler and DevTools.
  • Vendor Responsibilities & Operational Obligations
    Understand your obligations for customer support, maintenance, security practices, dependency updates, and long-term operational stewardship.
  • Diagrams

Vault enforces pipeline activation. You control everything else — licensing sales, entitlement management, token creation, validation, retry logic, and revocation.

Design Your Validation Strategy
↑ top

Before writing any code, you must decide how your licenses will be validated. Vault does not perform validation — it only enforces the result.

Your validation strategy may include:

  • Public/private key cryptographic verification
  • Signed JWT or HMAC-based tokens
  • Remote API validation via HTTPS
  • Offline license file verification
  • Hybrid models (local signature + remote entitlement check)

Your validation logic must ultimately produce a boolean result and call validateLicense(true | false).

You are responsible for retry behavior, revocation handling, expiration logic, network resilience, deduping multiple simultaneous validation requests, and cryptographic integrity.

Validation Scope & Licensing Models

You must also decide the scope of your license — whether it applies globally, per extension, or per FeatureCell instance. Vault enforces validation per extension instance, but your commercial model determines how you interpret and respond to those validation requests.

  • Per-FeatureCell validation — If your Behavior or Controller is installed in multiple FeatureCells, each instance will request validation independently. You are responsible for deduplicating remote calls if needed. This model allows seat-based or usage-based licensing, where you may limit how many FeatureCells are permitted to activate.
  • Seat-limited model — Because validation occurs per FeatureCell instance, you may enforce limits (for example, “5 active FeatureCells”). If the seat count is exceeded, return false for additional instances.
  • Shared license across multiple extensions — If you provide multiple Behaviors or Controllers that are sold as a single product, you may reuse the same licenseId across all of them. They can share a single entitlement decision.
  • Independent licensing per extension — If your Behaviors or Controllers are sold separately, assign unique licenseId values to enforce independent validation per extension.
  • Controller + Behavior working together — If a Controller and Behavior form a single product, reuse the same licenseId and validate once. Vault will enforce activation consistently across both.

Vault does not define your commercial scope. It simply enforces the boolean result you return for each registered extension instance. Whether that represents a global entitlement, a seat limit, or a per-extension product decision is entirely up to your validation logic.

Sell and Issue the License
↑ top

Monetization requires a commercial flow outside of Vault. You must define how customers purchase, receive, and manage licenses.

This typically includes:

  • Payment processing
  • License key or token generation
  • Customer entitlement tracking
  • Expiration rules
  • Revocation policies

Vault does not issue licenses, track customers, or enforce payments. That lifecycle belongs entirely to you.

When a customer completes a purchase, you provide them with the data required to activate your extension inside Vault.

Note

Vault is intentionally hands-off. It provides the enforcement mechanism — nothing more. It does not validate tokens, decrypt payloads, contact your servers, retry failures, or manage customer state.

All validation logic — cryptographic verification, remote API calls, entitlement checks, retry strategy, expiration handling, and revocation rules — is your responsibility. Vault simply accepts your true or false decision and enforces it deterministically.

Vault does not provide customer support for your extension. Questions related to license activation, validation failures, expired entitlements, cryptographic errors, or runtime behavior of your Behavior or Controller are your responsibility to diagnose and resolve. Vault enforces decisions — it does not troubleshoot your commercial implementation.

Define the License Payload
↑ top

The customer activates your extension by supplying the licenseId you issued along with an extension-specific payload during Vault configuration.

The payload is typed as unknown. Vault does not inspect, decrypt, or validate it. You fully define its structure and are solely responsible for parsing and verifying it inside your extension.

Common payload patterns include:

  • Signed JWT or token strings
  • Public/private key signatures
  • Customer or tenant identifiers
  • Encrypted license blobs
  • Entitlement metadata (plan, expiry, scope)

Choose a structure aligned with your validation strategy and hardened against tampering.

Note

The licenseId declared in your extension decorator must exactly match the licenseId provided in provideVault(). If they do not match, Vault will not inject the payload and validation cannot succeed.

Example: Vault Configuration

{{`provideVault({
  licenses: [
    {
      // Must match the licenseId declared in your extension
      licenseId: 'vendor-premium',
      payload: {
        token: 'signed-jwt-token',
        customerId: 'acme-123',
        plan: 'enterprise',
        expiresAt: '2026-12-31T23:59:59Z',
        signature: 'base64-signature'
      }
    }
  ]
});`}}

Example: Extension Decorator

{{`@VaultBehavior({
  type: BehaviorTypes.Merge,
  key: defineBehaviorKey('Vendor', 'PremiumMerge'),
  critical: false,
  needsLicense: true,
  // Must match the licenseId provided in provideVault()
  licenseId: 'vendor-premium'
})`}}
VaultLicensingShape
Property Description
licenseId: string Vendor-defined identifier used to associate a license payload with a specific Behavior or Controller. This value must match the licenseId declared in your extension decorator.
payload: unknown Opaque vendor-defined data supplied at Vault initialization. Vault stores and injects this payload but does not interpret it. Validation logic is entirely your responsibility.
Instruct the Customer How to Configure Vault
↑ top

Customers must provide your exact licenseId and payload during Vault initialization.

Your documentation should clearly instruct them how to configure:

  • The exact licenseId you issued
  • The required payload structure
  • Optional timeout configuration via licenseTimeoutMs (default is 15 seconds)

It is strongly recommended that you provide this configuration to your customer in a copy-paste ready format. The licenseId must match exactly, and payload structure errors will result in validation failure.

For larger payloads or enterprise environments, you may instruct customers to place the license entry in a dedicated file and import it into the licenses array. This reduces configuration mistakes and keeps sensitive data isolated.

If your validation process may exceed the default 15-second timeout, customers can increase the licenseTimeoutMs value during Vault initialization. However, long-running validation is strongly discouraged . License verification should resolve quickly and deterministically. Extended timeouts increase perceived startup latency and delay terminal enforcement. Design your validation strategy to complete within a predictable, bounded window whenever possible.

Example: Direct Configuration

{{`provideVault({
  licenses: [
    {
      licenseId: 'vendor-premium',
      payload: {
        token: 'signed-license-token'
      }
    }
  ],
  licenseTimeoutMs: 15000
});`}}

Example: Dedicated License File

You may instead provide customers with a pre-generated license file: 

{{`// vendor-premium.license.ts

import { VaultLicensingShape } from '@sdux-vault/shared';

export const vendorPremiumLicense: VaultLicensingShape = {
  licenseId: 'vendor-premium',
  payload: {
    token: 'signed-jwt-token',
    customerId: 'acme-123',
    plan: 'enterprise',
    expiresAt: '2026-12-31T23:59:59Z',
    signature: 'base64-signature'
  }
};`}}

The customer then imports and supplies it to Vault:

{{`import { vendorPremiumLicense } from './vendor-premium.license';

provideVault({
  licenses: [vendorPremiumLicense]
});`}}
Note

Without this configuration, Vault will treat your extension as pending and, after the configured timeout window, deny FeatureCell activation.

Required Contract
↑ top

1. Decorator Configuration

Your extension must declare both needsLicense: true and a licenseId: string. The licenseId is how Vault matches customer-supplied license payloads to your extension. 

{{`@VaultBehavior({
  type: BehaviorTypes.Merge,
  key: defineBehaviorKey('Vendor', 'PremiumMerge'),
  critical: false,
  needsLicense: true,
  licenseId: 'vendor-premium'
})`}}

The licenseId does not need to be globally unique. It must simply match the licenseId provided by the customer at Vault configuration time.

If you supply multiple licensed Behaviors or Controllers, you may reuse the same licenseId across all of them so they are validated together under a single entitlement. Alternatively, you may assign unique licenseId values to enforce independent licensing per extension. The choice depends entirely on your commercial model.

2. Extend LicensingAbstract

Your class must extend LicensingAbstract. This automatically:

  • Registers the extension with Vault
  • Requests a runtime license token
  • Protects against spoofed validation

3. Call validateLicense()

You must call validateLicense(true | false) once you have determined the validity of the license. If validateLicense() is never called, Vault will treat the license as pending and deny the FeatureCell after the configured timeout window.

  • Passing true indicates the license is valid and the extension may participate in the pipeline.
  • Passing false indicates the license is invalid or revoked and the Behavior or Controller must not execute.
Licensing Runtime Integration
↑ top

At runtime, Vault injects license data into your extension and enforces the validation result you provide.

When needsLicense: true is declared and a matching licenseId is provided in provideVault(), Vault injects the customer-supplied payload into your extension at instantiation time.

Your extension must interpret that payload, determine validity, and report the result to Vault. Vault does not inspect or validate payload data — it only enforces the boolean result you provide.

When a licensed extension is instantiated, Vault injects runtime licensing metadata and exposes a controlled validation surface. These runtime contracts define how your extension receives license data, how it reports validation results, and how Vault enforces those results.

The BehaviorClassContext provides access to the vendor-defined licensePayload supplied during provideVault(). Your extension is responsible for interpreting this payload, performing any necessary cryptographic or remote validation, and determining whether the license is valid.

BehaviorClassContext (Licensing)
Property Description
licensePayload?: unknown Vendor-defined license data injected by Vault at instantiation time when needsLicense: true is declared and a matching licenseId is supplied in provideVault().

Vault does not inspect, decrypt, validate, or transform this value. It is passed through as-is and made available to the extension via behaviorCtx.licensePayload.

The extension author is fully responsible for casting, validating, and securely interpreting this payload before reporting the result.

Once validation is complete, your extension must report the result using validateLicense(...). Vault does not inspect tokens or perform entitlement checks — it strictly enforces the boolean outcome you provide, using scoped identifiers and an internal license token to guarantee deterministic and non-spoofable enforcement.

Extension API: validateLicense()
Method Description

validateLicense(boolean)

input:

  • boolean

returns: void

Reports the final license validation result to Vault. This method must be called after your validation logic determines license validity.

  • true → License approved. The extension may participate in pipeline execution.
  • false → License invalid or revoked. The FeatureCell is terminal.

If validateLicense() is never called, Vault will treat the license as pending and deny the FeatureCell after the configured timeout window.

These mechanics guarantee deterministic enforcement while preserving complete vendor control over cryptographic validation.

Example: Licensed Behavior
↑ top

This example satisfies all requirements for a licensed Behavior.

  • needsLicense: true — Declares that this Behavior cannot participate in pipeline execution until a license decision is made.
  • licenseId — Provides the identifier Vault uses to inject the correct customer-supplied payload into this extension instance.
  • Extends LicensingAbstract<T> — Registers the Behavior with Vault’s licensing system, requests a runtime validation token, and protects against spoofed validation calls.
  • Implements BehaviorContract<T> — Ensures the Behavior conforms to the required pipeline contract (type, key, critical flag, lifecycle hooks).
  • Implements computeMerge() — Satisfies the required contract for BehaviorTypes.Merge by defining how upstream values are combined during the Merge stage. Each pipeline stage requires its own contract-specific methods to be implemented.
  • Implements destroy() and reset() — Satisfies the lifecycle contract. Even if no cleanup is required, these methods must be present.
  • Calls validateLicense(isValid) — After determining license validity, the extension explicitly notifies Vault. This is the only mechanism that transitions the extension from pending to valid or revoked.
Note

Once validateLicense(true) is called, the Behavior is permitted to participate in the pipeline. If false is supplied, the FeatureCell along with the pipeline is terminal.

The validation logic may be synchronous (as shown) or asynchronous. If asynchronous, it must complete within the configured timeout window (default: 15 seconds), or Vault will deny activation automatically. 

{{`@VaultBehavior({
  // This behavior participates in the Merge stage of the pipeline.
  type: BehaviorTypes.Merge,

  // Unique identifier used internally for correlation and diagnostics.
  key: defineBehaviorKey('Vendor', 'PremiumMerge'),

  // If true, errors would hard-stop the pipeline.
  // Licensing failures should resolve via validateLicense(false), not by throwing.
  critical: false,

  // Declares that this behavior requires successful license validation
  // before it may participate in pipeline execution.
  needsLicense: true,

  // Must exactly match the licenseId supplied in provideVault().
  // Vault uses this value to inject the correct license payload.
  licenseId: 'vendor-premium'
})
export class withPremiumMerge<T>
  extends LicensingAbstract<T>
  implements BehaviorContract<T> {

  // Required static metadata for pipeline registration.
  static readonly type: BehaviorType;
  static readonly critical = false;

  // Instance-level bindings used by the orchestrator.
  readonly type = withPremiumMerge.type;
  readonly critical = withPremiumMerge.critical;
  readonly key: string;

  constructor(key: string, readonly ctx: BehaviorClassContext) {
    // Registers the behavior with Vault’s licensing system
    // and requests a license token.
    super(ctx);

    this.key = key;

    // ----------------------------------------------------------
    // Vendor validation logic
    // ----------------------------------------------------------
    // You are responsible for verifying:
    // - Cryptographic signatures
    // - Token expiration
    // - Remote entitlement status
    // - Revocation rules
    //
    // Vault does not validate the payload.
    // Vault only enforces the boolean result you provide.
    const isValid = MyVendorLicenseService().verify();

    // Notify Vault of the final validation result.
    // true  → behavior may participate in the pipeline
    // false → FeatureCell will be denied
    this.validateLicense(isValid);
  }

  // Required for BehaviorTypes.Merge.
  // Defines how upstream values are combined during the Merge stage.
  computeMerge(
    current: T | undefined,
    next: T | undefined
  ): T | undefined {
    return next;
  }

  // Lifecycle hooks required by BehaviorContract.
  // Use these for cleanup or state reset logic if needed.
  destroy() {}

  reset() {}
}`}}
Example: Licensed Controller
↑ top

This example satisfies all requirements for a licensed Controller.

  • needsLicense: true — Declares that this Controller cannot participate in Policy-stage decisions until license validation completes.
  • licenseId — Identifies which customer-supplied payload Vault should inject into this Controller instance during instantiation.
  • Extends LicensingAbstract<T> — Registers the Controller with Vault’s licensing system, obtains a secure runtime token, and prevents spoofed validation calls.
  • Implements ControllerContract<T> — Ensures the Controller conforms to Policy-stage execution requirements.
  • Implements handleMessage() — Provides the Policy-stage vote logic. In this example, the Controller abstains, meaning it does not block or alter execution.
  • Implements destroy() and reset() — Satisfies the lifecycle contract. Even if no cleanup is required, these methods must exist.
  • Calls validateLicense(...) — Once license validity is determined, the Controller explicitly notifies Vault. This is the only mechanism that transitions the extension from pending to valid or revoked.
Note

Once validateLicense(true) is called, the Controller is permitted to participate in the pipeline. If false is supplied, the FeatureCell and pipeline becomes terminal.

The validation logic may be synchronous (as shown) or asynchronous. If asynchronous, it must complete within the configured timeout window (default: 15 seconds), or Vault will deny activation automatically. 

{{`@VaultController({
  // This controller participates in the Policy stage of the pipeline.
  type: ControllerTypes.Policy,

  // Unique identifier for this controller instance.
  // Used internally by Vault for correlation and enforcement.
  key: defineControllerKey('Vendor', 'PremiumPolicy'),

  // If true, any thrown error would hard-stop the pipeline.
  // Licensing failures should be handled via validateLicense(false),
  // not by throwing.
  critical: false,

  // Declares that this controller cannot execute until license validation succeeds.
  needsLicense: true,

  // Must exactly match the licenseId provided in provideVault().
  // Vault uses this to inject the correct license payload.
  licenseId: 'vendor-premium'
})
export class withPremiumPolicy<T>
  extends LicensingAbstract<T>
  implements ControllerContract<T> {

  // Required static metadata for pipeline registration.
  static readonly type: ControllerType;
  static readonly critical = false;

  // Instance-level bindings used by the orchestrator.
  readonly type = withPremiumPolicy.type;
  readonly critical = withPremiumPolicy.critical;
  readonly key: string;

  constructor(key: string, readonly ctx: ControllerClassContext) {
    // Registers the controller with Vault’s licensing system
    // and requests a license token.
    super(ctx);

    this.key = key;

    // ----------------------------------------------------------
    // Vendor validation logic
    // ----------------------------------------------------------
    // You are responsible for verifying:
    // - Cryptographic signatures
    // - Token expiration
    // - Remote entitlement status
    // - Revocation rules
    //
    // Vault does not validate the payload.
    // Vault only enforces the boolean result you provide.
    const isValid = MyVendorLicenseService().verify();

    // Notify Vault of the final validation result.
    // true  → controller may participate in pipeline execution
    // false → FeatureCell will be denied
    this.validateLicense(isValid);
  }

  // Policy controllers must implement handleMessage().
  // Returning Abstain means this controller does not block execution.
  handleMessage(): Observable<ControllerVote> {
    return of(ControllerVotes.Abstain);
  }

  // Lifecycle hooks required by ControllerContract.
  // Use these to clean up resources, cancel subscriptions, etc.
  destroy() {}

  reset() {}
}`}}
Asynchronous Validation
↑ top

When validating your license payload, you are responsible for performing any required cryptographic verification, token decryption, signature checks, expiration validation, or remote entitlement calls before invoking validateLicense().

What This Example Does Correctly

  • Uses the injected licensePayload — The extension retrieves the Vault-injected payload from behaviorCtx and explicitly casts it to a vendor-defined request shape.
  • Separates validation logic from the constructor — The constructor delegates to a dedicated performLicenseValidation() method, keeping instantiation clean and validation concerns isolated.
  • Defines explicit request and response contracts — Typed interfaces (LicenseValidationRequest and LicenseValidationResponse) make the remote validation boundary predictable and self-documenting.
  • Performs deterministic async validation — The extension awaits the remote entitlement check and resolves to a single boolean outcome.
  • Fails closed — Any network, parsing, or runtime error results in validateLicense(false), ensuring the pipeline does not remain in an indeterminate state.
  • Calls validateLicense() exactly once — The extension reports a final validation result after the async process completes, allowing Vault to enforce activation or denial deterministically.
  • Exports a shared payload contract — By exporting LicenseValidationRequest, the vendor provides a strongly typed contract that customers can use when constructing their provideVault() license entry. This reduces configuration errors, enforces payload shape consistency, and improves integration reliability.

Timeout Requirement

Asynchronous validation must complete within the configured timeout window (default: 15 seconds). If validation does not resolve before timeout, Vault will deny the FeatureCell.

Failure Handling

Your validation logic must always resolve deterministically. If an async operation throws, rejects, or fails, you must explicitly call validateLicense(false) or implement your own retry strategy.

Vault does not retry, recover, or compensate for failed validation attempts.

Asynchronous Validation Example

{{`// -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Shared Contract: Exported for Customer Type Safety
// -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Export this interface so customers can correctly type their Vault
// configuration payload when calling provideVault().

export interface LicenseValidationRequest {
  token: string;        // Signed license token issued by vendor
  customerId: string;   // Unique customer or tenant identifier
}

// Internal response shape returned by your validation service.
interface LicenseValidationResponse {
  valid: boolean;       // Final entitlement decision
}

constructor(
  key: string,
  readonly behaviorCtx: BehaviorClassContext
) {
  // Registers the behavior with Vault and requests a license token.
  // Vault injects \`licensePayload\` at this point if a matching licenseId exists.
  super(behaviorCtx);

  this.key = key;

  // Perform validation immediately upon instantiation.
  // The extension must eventually call validateLicense(true | false).
  this.performLicenseValidation();
}

private async performLicenseValidation(): Promise<void> {
  try {
    // -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    // 1. Retrieve the Vault-injected payload
    // -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    // Vault does NOT validate this object.
    // You are fully responsible for casting and verifying it.
    const payload = this.behaviorCtx.licensePayload as LicenseValidationRequest;

    // Defensive safeguard — if payload is missing or malformed,
    // resolve deterministically as invalid.
    if (!payload) {
      this.validateLicense(false);
      return;
    }

    // -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    // 2. Construct your validation request
    // -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    // Only send the data required for entitlement verification.
    const request: LicenseValidationRequest = {
      token: payload.token,
      customerId: payload.customerId
    };

    // -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    // 3. Call your entitlement service
    // -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    // This may perform:
    // - Signature verification
    // - Expiration checks
    // - Revocation checks
    // - Subscription status validation
    const response = await fetch('/api/license/verify', {
      method: 'POST',
      headers: {
        'Content-Type': 'application/json'
      },
      body: JSON.stringify(request)
    });

    const result: LicenseValidationResponse = await response.json();

    // -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    // 4. Report final decision to Vault
    // -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    // true  → Behavior may participate in pipeline execution
    // false → FeatureCell becomes denied (terminal)
    this.validateLicense(result.valid);

  } catch {
    // -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    // Any failure must resolve deterministically.
    // Vault will NOT retry for you.
    // Network failure, malformed response, cryptographic error —
    // all must end in a clear true/false decision.
    // -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    this.validateLicense(false);
  }
}`}}

Customer Typed Example

{{`// Type-safe license payload supplied to Vault.
// The shape must match the contract expected by the licensed extension.
const payload: LicenseValidationRequest = {
  token: 'signed-jwt-token',
  customerId: 'acme-123'
};

provideVault({
  licenses: [
    {
      licenseId: 'vendor-premium',
      payload
    }
  ]
});`}}
Runtime Guarantees
↑ top

Vault’s licensing system enforces a strict, deterministic state model at runtime. Once a FeatureCell contains licensed extensions, activation is governed entirely by validation outcomes and timeout rules. The guarantees below define exactly how Vault transitions a FeatureCell from pending to active or terminal.

  • If any licensed extension fails → FeatureCell is terminal.
  • If validation never occurs → timeout → terminal.
  • If all validate → FeatureCell activates.
  • If none require license → automatic activation.
  • State updates received while validation is pending are queued.
    Once the FeatureCell activates, all queued updates are processed in order.
  • After terminal denial → no resurrection.
State machine:
License Enforcement Outcomes
↑ top

Vault enforces licensing deterministically. The table below summarizes how validation outcomes affect FeatureCell activation.

License Validation Outcomes
Scenario Result
Validation returns false FeatureCell is terminal and pipeline execution stops.
Validation never called Timeout window expires → FeatureCell is terminal.
Timeout reached FeatureCell is terminal.
All licensed extensions valid FeatureCell activates normally.
Late validation after denial Ignored. FeatureCell terminal state cannot be reversed.

If a FeatureCell contains multiple licensed extensions, all must validate successfully. A single failure results in denial of the entire pipeline.

Architectural Guarantees
↑ top

The licensing model is intentionally strict and clearly separated by responsibility:

Responsibility Boundaries
Component Responsibility
Vault Deterministic reducer and enforcement engine.
Vendor Cryptographic authority and validation logic owner.
Timeout Liveness guarantee preventing indefinite pending states.
Terminal Denial No resurrection after a license is terminal. Final and irreversible.

Vault never performs cryptographic verification. Vendors never control enforcement. This separation prevents spoofing, eliminates race conditions, and guarantees deterministic activation behavior.

Failure Handling & Observability
↑ top

When a license fails:

  • The pipeline is terminal.
  • The global error handler is notified.
  • DevTools displays the denial (when enabled).

Vendors are responsible for handling retry logic, token refresh, and network resilience inside their own validation implementation.

In addition, when validation fails, it is recommended that your extension make an asynchronous call to your backend or monitoring service to record the failure. This allows you to detect revoked licenses, expired entitlements, misconfigurations, or potential abuse in real time.

Vault enforces denial deterministically, but vendor-side observability ensures you can investigate, support the customer, and respond appropriately.

Vendor Responsibilities & Operational Obligations
↑ top

Monetizing a Behavior or Controller means you are operating as a software vendor. provides enforcement infrastructure — it does not assume responsibility for your commercial, operational, or security practices.

As the extension author, you are responsible for:

  • Defining and enforcing your commercial license agreement
  • Managing customer purchases, renewals, upgrades, and revocation
  • Issuing and rotating license keys or signed payloads
  • Maintaining secure cryptographic validation practices
  • Handling network failures, retries, and degraded service scenarios
  • Providing customer support for installation and activation issues
  • Maintaining compatibility with new versions of
  • Keeping npm dependencies and cryptographic libraries up to date
  • Monitoring security advisories and responding to vulnerabilities

Vault guarantees deterministic enforcement of validation results. It does not guarantee commercial correctness, entitlement accuracy, network availability, or security posture.

If your validation service is compromised, misconfigured, or offline, your extension will fail validation — and the FeatureCell will be denied.

SQX reserves the right to suspend or revoke distribution of third-party extensions that introduce security risks, violate ecosystem policies, or negatively impact platform stability. Maintaining operational integrity and customer trust is a non-negotiable requirement for participation in the ecosystem.

Design your validation and deployment strategy accordingly.

Relation to SDuX Ecosystem Licensing
